title: The Mysterious Disappearance of the Franklin Expedition
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck cover the 1845 Franklin Expedition, the British Royal Navy voyage led by Captain John Franklin to chart the last uncharted stretch of the Northwest Passage in the Canadian Arctic. The expedition's ships, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror, were iced in, and all 129 crew were lost. The episode covers Franklin's earlier expeditions (including eating his boots), Lady Jane Franklin's role in securing the command, the ships' steam engines, central heating and supplies (tinned food, lemon juice, pemmican), the whaling ships that last saw them, the ice and "warping" navigation, the deaths and theories (lead poisoning, botulism, scurvy, bad weather), the Inuit oral history, John Rae's cannibalism report and the backlash against it, the 1850s search period and reward, and the discovery of the wrecks in 2014 and 2016. The episode ends with a listener mail short about the Montfort lane truckers' term.

segments.title: Opening banter and overview
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Franklin Expedition as a famous Arctic disaster in which all 129 crew were lost, and mention the AMC series The Terror.

segments.title: Northwest Passage and Royal Navy mapping goals
segments.summary: The Northwest Passage is described as hard to traverse because of moving ice. The Royal Navy wanted to chart the last blank part of the Arctic, and earlier explorers such as Robert McClure and Roald Amundsen are mentioned. Franklin's expedition contributed to charting while lost.

segments.title: John Franklin's early career and earlier expeditions
segments.summary: Franklin's background as a poor-born naval officer who turned to Arctic exploration after downsizing. His second expedition ended in failure, and he became famous for eating his boots, and he was knighted. Inuit helped his earlier expeditions survive, and the hosts discuss how Europeans ignored Inuit knowledge.

segments.title: Lady Jane Franklin and the appointment
segments.summary: Franklin, in his fifties and after a Tasmania posting, is persuaded by his wife Lady Jane Franklin to lead one more expedition to chart the Northwest Passage. Hosts discuss whether the post was undesirable.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Franklin's leadership record
segments.summary: Josh says Franklin was an average captain, neither the best nor worst, and that Lady Jane's influence got him the job. Hosts joke about captain names.

segments.title: Ships Erebus and Terror and their steam engines
segments.summary: The two ships were retrofitted with iron plates for ice, and a steam engine as a boost. They also had central heating and a water distillation system, and retractable propellers.

segments.title: Expedition supplies and animals
segments.summary: The ships carried beef, tinned meat, fresh vegetables, livestock, and pets including a monkey, a Newfoundland dog named Neptune, and a cat.

segments.title: Sugar, tobacco, alcohol, candles, and lemon juice
segments.summary: Supplies included sugar, spices, tobacco, alcohol, candles, and about 900 gallons of lemon juice to prevent scurvy. Historians theorize boiling may have made the juice ineffective.

segments.title: Tinned food and pemmican
segments.summary: The expedition ordered canned food from contractor Stephen Goldner, a new technology. Pemmican, a dried meat and fat paste, is described.

segments.title: Departure from Disko Bay and whaling ship sightings
segments.summary: The expedition took on supplies in Disko Bay, Greenland, and left five men there. Whaling ships Enterprise and Prince of Wales last saw them before Lancaster Sound.

segments.title: Ice navigation, warping, and first winter
segments.summary: Explanation of ice navigation and warping. The first winter and summer went fine, though three men died. Ships were stuck in ice.

segments.title: Second winter, Franklin's death, and the note
segments.summary: The ships were iced in off King William Island. A note in a cairn reported Franklin died June 11 (1847). Crozier and Fitzjames were next in command.

segments.title: Abandoning the ships and walking toward safety
segments.summary: Crozier chose to abandon the ships and walk toward safety after ice failed to melt. Some Inuit reached mainland Canada.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Search expeditions and the reward
segments.summary: The search period from 1847 to 1859 drew over thirty expeditions. The Royal Navy offered a reward of 20,000 pounds. John Rae reported Inuit accounts of cannibalism, which Lady Jane Franklin and Charles Dickens denounced.

segments.title: Discovery of the Erebus and Terror wrecks
segments.summary: Erebus was found in 2014 and Terror in 2016 in shallow water, fairly intact. Parks Canada divers documented the wrecks, and documents may remain in drawers.

segments.title: Causes of death: weather, underpreparation, and lead
segments.summary: Theories include bad weather, underpreparation, and heavy equipment. Ice core samples showed the winters were among the worst in 700 years. Lead contamination from tin solder is discussed, following Owen Beatty's 1981 study.

segments.title: Botulism, survivors, and cannibalism evidence
segments.summary: Possible botulism from contaminated tins is discussed. Inuit reports describe four survivors and a dog in 1851-52. Physical evidence of cannibalism includes cut and broken bones; John Geiger documented that Inuit accounts were ignored.

segments.title: Wrap-up and mention of Nova
segments.summary: Hosts summarize, note new wreck information may come, and recommend a Nova episode.

segments.title: Listener mail: Montfort lane
segments.summary: Listener Kent writes about the 1970s trucker term Montfort lane, the left lane of the interstate, linked to Kenny Montfort's meat-hauling fleet. The Montfort family later co-owned the Colorado Rockies.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and invite listeners to send short stuff submissions.
